name: Lactobionic acid

lead: Lactobionic acid is a sugar acid made by oxidising lactose, grouped in cosmetics with the polyhydroxy acids (PHAs). It is sold as a milder alternative to glycolic and lactic acid, for smoother, hydrated, softer-looking skin, and is described as moisturising and antioxidant.

Its many hydroxyl groups let it bind water and chelate metals such as iron, which is the basis of the antioxidant claim. It is a large molecule, which proponents say explains slower penetration and lower irritation. Most published work concerns organ-preservation fluids, food additives and drug carriers; skincare claims rest mainly on descriptive and review literature.

paras: It is used in serums, creams and mild peels, typically on a regular routine for gradual smoothing and hydration, with sun protection alongside.

Topical products using it are generally described as well tolerated. As with other exfoliating acids, sun protection is advised on labels. Its approved medical roles, organ-preservation solutions and erythromycin lactobionate, are unrelated to cosmetic use.

angle.text: Lactobionic acid is a gentle polyhydroxy acid used for smoother, hydrated skin with less stinging than stronger acids. It exfoliates mildly while binding water to the surface, leaving skin softer and brighter-looking; its chemistry is well documented, and published skin trials are few.

lead: Lactobionic acid (LBA) is a disaccharide sugar acid formed from galactose linked to gluconic acid, and can be made by oxidising lactose.[1] It is freely soluble in water and forms salts with calcium, potassium, sodium and zinc.[1]

In skincare it is classed as a polyhydroxy acid (PHA), marketed as a gentler relative of alpha hydroxy acids, and is described as having moisturising and antioxidant properties.[2] Outside cosmetics, its salts are used as a food stabiliser (calcium lactobionate, E399), in organ-preservation solutions, and as the counter-ion in intravenous erythromycin.[1][3]

No published randomised trial in the sources reviewed tests lactobionic acid specifically for appearance outcomes. Claims about skin benefits are drawn mainly from descriptive and in-vitro literature.

paras: Lactobionic acid is 4-O-beta-galactopyranosyl-D-gluconic acid, a syrup-like substance when isolated and freely water soluble.[1] Descriptions note that it carries eight hydroxyl groups and a carboxylic acid group, giving it strong water-binding behaviour, and a pKa near 3.8.[2] Production routes include microbial fermentation of dairy by-products such as whey, enzymatic synthesis, and chemical oxidation.[2]

Cosmetic descriptions present lactobionic acid as an exfoliant that increases cell turnover gently, a humectant and an antioxidant, and mention use after procedures such as peels to soothe skin.[2] Wikipedia notes its cosmetic use as an antioxidant in topical emulsions.[1] Alongside gluconolactone it is the PHA most often named in this context.[2]

Potassium lactobionate is a component of organ-preservation solutions (University of Wisconsin solution and similar), where it acts as an impermeant that limits cell swelling during cold storage.[1][4][3] Erythromycin lactobionate is the intravenous form of that antibiotic.[1] Calcium lactobionate serves as a food stabiliser.[1] Research literature also uses it to target nanoparticles and gene carriers to liver cells via galactose recognition.[5]

No studies found for lactobionic acid as a topical cosmetic agent in the sources reviewed. Related clinical work concerns organ-preservation solutions containing lactobionate, which has been studied in transplantation for decades,[4][3] and clinical trials that only list lactobionate-containing compounds (such as erythromycin lactobionate) are not studies of skin effects.

The Wikipedia entry gives no toxicity data.[1] For the broader alpha hydroxy acid family, the FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review have said such products are generally safe at low concentrations and pH above 3.5 with safety instructions, noting mild irritation, redness and flaking as the most common effects and increased sunburn likelihood that reverses after stopping.[6] Proponents of PHAs say lactobionic acid is less irritating than smaller acids; this has been asserted in review descriptions rather than shown in head-to-head trials in the sources reviewed.[2]

timeline.event: Lactobionic acid first produced by bacterial oxidation of lactose, according to Grokipedia.[2]
Studies on the components of the University of Wisconsin preservation solution, which contains lactobionate, are published.[4]
